The basic idea is simple: when you earn interest on your account, that interest gets added to your balance. Next period, you earn interest on the new, larger balance—including the interest you just received. The cycle repeats, so your money grows faster and faster.

\[
\$1,000 \times (1 + 0.005) = \$1,005.
\]

In the second month you earn 0.5% on \$1,005, not the original \$1,000. Your balance becomes:

\[
\$1,005 \times (1 + 0.005) = \$1,010.03.
\]

Each month the interest amount grows a little, so the curve bends upward.

The seasons on Earth are caused by the tilt of its rotation axis relative to its orbital plane around the Sun, a tilt of about 23.5 degrees. This tilt means that during different parts of the year, one hemisphere leans toward the Sun while the other leans away.

When a hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, sunlight strikes it more directly and daylight lasts longer, so the ground and atmosphere absorb more heat—this is summer. At the same time, the opposite hemisphere tilts away, receiving weaker sunlight and shorter days—its winter. Six months later the situation reverses, producing the familiar cycle.

The distance from Earth to the Sun changes only slightly over the year and is not the main driver; in fact, Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during the northern hemisphere’s winter, showing that proximity is not the cause.

The tilt also sets the solstices, when one pole points most directly at the Sun (longest day in that hemisphere) and the opposite pole points most away (shortest day). Equinoxes occur when the tilt is sideways relative to the Sun, giving roughly equal day and night everywhere.

The primary cause of Earth’s seasons is the tilt of its rotational axis relative to the plane of its orbit around the sun. This axial tilt—about 23.4 degrees—means that, over the course of a year, different hemispheres receive varying angles and durations of sunlight. When the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the sun, sunlight strikes it more directly and days are longer, producing summer; six months later the tilt reverses, causing winter. The same geometry applies to the Southern Hemisphere, but the seasons are opposite.

The tilt itself stays nearly constant in direction, pointing toward Polaris throughout the year, so as Earth orbits the sun the orientation of the tilt relative to the sun changes. That changing orientation, not the distance from the sun, drives seasonal temperature differences. In fact, Earth is slightly closer to the sun in January (perihelion) than in July, yet the Northern Hemisphere experiences winter in January, showing that distance plays only a minor role.

The seasons arise because Earth’s axis is tilted about 23.5° relative to the plane of its orbit, not because the planet gets closer to or farther from the Sun. As Earth travels around the Sun each year, the tilt keeps the same orientation in space, so different hemispheres receive more direct sunlight at different times.

In summer, a hemisphere tilts toward the Sun. Sunlight strikes more vertically, concentrating energy over a smaller area and lengthening the day. In winter, the same hemisphere tilts away; the Sun’s rays arrive at a shallow angle, spreading energy over a larger surface and shortening daylight hours. Spring and autumn occur at the equinoxes when the tilt is sideways to the Sun, giving roughly equal day and night.

This tilt-driven cycle also explains why the seasons in the Northern and Southern hemispheres are opposite: when one side is tilted toward the Sun, the other is tilted away.

The Milankovitch cycles—slow variations in Earth’s eccentricity, axial tilt, and precession—modify the pattern over tens of thousands of years, but the 23.5° tilt is the immediate cause of the yearly seasons we experience.

Procrastination isn’t laziness—it’s an emotion-regulation problem. You’re postponing the task because it feels threatening, boring, or overwhelming. The trick is to shrink the task, lower the fear, and give yourself immediate payoff.

**1. Turn the task into a 5-minute experiment**  
Set a timer for five minutes and commit to doing only that much. Write a single sentence, open the spreadsheet, clean one shelf. Once the timer rings, you’re free to quit. Most people find they keep going because the dread was bigger than the work.

**2. Pair the task with a reward you actually want**  
Only allow yourself a favorite podcast, coffee, or list of music while the task is happening. If the work stops, the reward stops. This creates a tiny dopamine loop that makes the task feel less like punishment.

**3. Use “body doubling”**  
Work alongside another person—physically or virtually. The mere presence of someone else doing something productive raises your own sense of accountability. A coworker’s Zoom square, a study group, or a library table can keep you honest without any extra pressure.

Setting up a monthly budget doesn’t have to feel like a tax audit — it’s just a shopping list for your money. Start with the big picture: write down every dollar you bring in each month (after tax). If your paycheck varies, use the lowest number you’re confident you’ll hit.

Next, list the fixed bills that arrive like clockwork: rent or mortgage, car loan, phone plan, insurance, subscriptions. These are your “must-pay” anchors.

After that, estimate variable costs you can control: groceries, gas, eating out, hobbies. Grab last month’s bank statement if you need a baseline, then round up slightly so you’re not caught short.

Then carve out space for debt payments and savings. Treat savings like a non-negotiable bill — even $50 a month adds up to $600 by year-end.

Finally, leave a small buffer for surprises. If the budget balances to zero, you’ve won; if you’re over, trim the variable items first before touching fixed ones.

You can fix it yourself with basic tools, but first identify your faucet type: compression (two handles), ball (single handle, dome top), cartridge (single handle, lever), or ceramic disc (smooth single lever). For the common single-handle cartridge model, start by shutting off the water under the sink and unplugging the disposal so nothing spins while you work.
